lines.text:
Open Wide — A Visit to the Dentist

Most people visit the dentist twice a year, but many are still nervous about it. Understanding what happens during a visit — and learning the vocabulary — can make the experience less frightening.

The dental chair is the centre of the room. It reclines so the dentist can see inside your mouth. An overhead light shines brightly. A rinse bowl sits to one side — you use it to rinse and spit after the cleaning. A tray table holds the instruments. The armrest and headrest keep you comfortable. A monitor on the wall may show your X-rays. A foot pedal controls the drill speed. The cuspidor — a small sink near the chair — collects water. An instrument panel displays controls for the dentist. Nearby, a dental stool on wheels lets the dentist sit at the right height.

The dentist uses many small instruments. A dental mirror — angled and round — reflects light into dark corners of the mouth. A probe checks each tooth for soft spots that might be cavities. A scaler scrapes plaque — the sticky layer of bacteria — from the teeth and gum line. A polisher smooths and shines the tooth surface after cleaning. A dental pick removes food stuck between teeth. Tweezers hold small items. A syringe delivers anaesthetic (numbing injection) before painful procedures.

If the dentist finds a cavity, a dental drill removes the damaged part of the tooth. A filling tool places the filling material — usually composite resin — into the hole. An excavator removes softened decay. A burnisher smooths the filling. An amalgam carrier delivers metal filling material. A dental spatula mixes materials. A rubber dam isolates the tooth being worked on. A bite block keeps the mouth open. A matrix band wraps around the tooth to shape the filling.

All instruments are cleaned in a steriliser or autoclave — a machine that uses high-pressure steam to kill all bacteria. Hygiene is the most important rule in a dental practice.

The X-ray machine takes pictures of the teeth and jaw to find problems below the surface. A dental lamp provides extra light for detailed work.

At home, the dentist recommends daily care. A toothbrush — manual or electric — cleans the tooth surfaces. Toothpaste contains fluoride, which strengthens enamel. Dental floss cleans between teeth. Mouthwash kills bacteria and freshens breath. Fluoride gel provides extra protection. Dental wax smooths the edges of braces. A retainer holds teeth in place after orthodontic treatment. A mouth guard protects teeth during sports. Whitening strips lighten the colour. An interdental brush cleans between wider gaps. Denture cleaner is for patients with false teeth. Desensitising paste helps with sensitive teeth. Dental cement repairs temporary damage. A temporary filling protects a tooth between appointments. A night guard prevents grinding during sleep.

The dentist's message is always the same: brush twice a day, floss daily, and come back in six months.

lines.text: In the UK, dental treatment is available through the National Health Service (NHS) at reduced cost, but not free for adults. Children, pregnant women, and people on low incomes receive free NHS dental treatment. Private dentistry is more expensive but often has shorter waiting times.

lines.text: In English-speaking countries, when a child loses a baby tooth, they place it under their pillow at night. The 'Tooth Fairy' takes the tooth and leaves a small amount of money. This tradition is often referenced in children's books and films.

lines.text: 'Dentist' = general dental practitioner. 'Dental surgeon' = performs surgical procedures. 'Orthodontist' = specialises in straightening teeth (braces). 'Periodontist' = specialises in gum disease. These distinctions appear in B2 health vocabulary.

lines.text: Modal verbs + bare infinitive — no 'to.' 'I must brush.' 'You should floss.' 'We can wait.' This applies to all modals without exception. If you want to use 'to': 'I have to brush', 'I need to floss' — but these are not modal verbs.

lines.text: 'Pain' is usually a noun in English, not a verb. 'I have pain in my tooth.' 'My tooth hurts.' 'My tooth is aching.' 'I'm in pain.' 'The pain is getting worse.' As a verb, 'pain' is mostly literary: 'It pains me to say this.' For physical discomfort, use 'hurt' or 'ache.'

lines.text: 'Afraid of + noun/-ing': 'afraid of the dentist', 'afraid of going.' Never 'afraid from.' Other common adjective + preposition: 'nervous about', 'worried about', 'scared of', 'anxious about.' Each adjective has its own fixed preposition.

lines.text: 'Every' + time period for regular intervals: 'every six months', 'every day', 'every year.' 'Each' emphasises individual items: 'each tooth', 'each patient.' For frequency, 'every' is standard: 'every morning', 'every two weeks.' 'Each' + number is non-standard.
